name: Bianca Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me is confidential and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I walk over to the Brandts' at seven, it's ten minutes across the lane. I let the hens out, collect the eggs, then I help Jakob, that's their son, with the sheep, about a hundred and fifty ewes. In autumn it's lifting potatoes and in summer it's the oats. Jakob is thirty and he's teaching me, which is a funny thing at my age, but he's patient. I'm still slow with the sheep, I can't catch one to save my life.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you do before working on the farm?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was a seamstress for thirty-two years at the uniform factory in town. Then they moved the sewing abroad and that was that. The Brandts have sat two pews in front of us at St Mark's for twenty years, and when Mrs Brandt heard, she said come and work for us. The pay is low, and Klaus only does part-time caretaking at the church, so we get by, just. We've never had much in the bank, but we've never taken a penny from anyone either.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use computers or AI at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No. Never have. My daughter wanted to put one of those talking things on my phone and I told her no thank you. If I want to know something, I ask a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, good. I never believed all that anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there you are, it was all talk, just like I said. After church I'd say it to the women doing the teas, and they'd agree with me. I don't go online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means things go on as they are, and that suits me. The Brandts need someone for the hens and the sheep, and I'm getting better, slowly. A plateau, if that's the word, is fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on just as I am. Get up, walk over the lane, do the hens. Maybe I'd ask Jakob to teach me the lambing properly this spring, because I only watched last year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really, apart from the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said apart from the money. How tight is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight. We pay the rent and the heating, and that's most of it. If the boiler went, I'd have to ask my son, and I'd rather go cold for a week first. Klaus says I'm too proud. I say we were raised to manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you like best about working at the Brandts'?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's people who know you. At the factory, at the end, it was a man from head office who'd never seen our town. At the Brandts', if I'm poorly, Mrs Brandt brings soup. You don't get that from a company.

S0.say: I'd tell the women doing the church teas that it was all talk, just as I said. I don't go online.
S0.think: Things go on as they are, which suits me. The farm needs someone for the hens and sheep, and I'm slowly getting better at it.
S0.do: Carries on with her routine at the neighbours' farm. Asks the farmer's son to teach her lambing properly this spring.
S0.feel: Calm and content, apart from money worries.
S0.quote: If the boiler went, I'd have to ask my son, and I'd rather go cold for a week first.
S0.fieldNote: Bianca's life rests on loyalty: her job came through church friendship with the farm family. She is proud of never having taken help, even from her own son. She contrasts the Brandts' kindness with a distant head office that closed her factory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds more like real life, I'll grant you. Things change slowly whether we like it or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should work hard and learn what they need to, and not expect the government to carry them. That's what I'd say at church and to my family. Hard work and family, that's always been the answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the Brandts would keep me as long as they could, because that's the kind of people they are. But Jakob's young, he reads about these things, he might want a machine for the hens. I'm not sure what I'd do then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work harder, turn up early, show them I'm worth keeping. I'd not go learning computers, I'm too old for that. But I'd try to put a bit aside each week, even five, in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Like something's coming down the lane and I can't see it yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd not learn computers. If Jakob asked you to learn a machine for the hens, would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If he asked, I'd try, because you don't say no to the people who took you in. But I'd be no good at it, and he'd know. That's the bit that worries me, being a burden to them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your children about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them nothing unless they asked. They've got their own lives. My son has his garage and two little ones. I'm not going to fill his ears with worry about robots.

S1.say: I'd say people should work hard and learn what they need to, not expect the government to carry them. Hard work and family have always been the answer.
S1.think: The Brandts would keep me as long as they could, but their son might want a machine for the hens. I'm not sure what I'd do then.
S1.do: Works harder and arrives earlier to show she's worth keeping. Saves 5 a week, and would try a new machine only if the farmer's son asked.
S1.feel: Uneasy, as if something is coming down the lane that she can't yet see.
S1.quote: If he asked, I'd try, because you don't say no to the people who took you in.
S1.fieldNote: Bianca's public line is self-reliance and family over government. Privately her fear is less about losing pay than about becoming a burden to the family who took her in. She'd keep worries from her children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? Then it's in God's hands, because it's too quick for mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when people chase money and forget about people. I'd say it after church. I'd say families and churches need to look after each other, because I don't trust government to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, if the robots can do everything, even the Brandts can't afford to keep me. They'd want to, but they've got the bank to pay too. I'd be 60, with nothing put by and no other work in the town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go back to sewing. Alterations, curtains, mending, for people in the parish, for a bit of cash. I'd cut the heating and the car. And if it came to it, I'd ask my son for help, and the church has a hardship fund, though it would break my heart to use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd pray about it, but I'd be frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't trust government. Would you take government help if it was there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it was there and I'd paid in, yes, I suppose I'd have to. Forty years of tax. But I'd rather it came through the church or family. Help from people who know you is different from a form.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does two years' warning change things, compared with more time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, there's no getting to the pension, no getting to anything. I'd just be standing there with my sewing box. If it were ten years, I'd be at home with Klaus by then, and it wouldn't touch me.

S2.say: I'd say this is what happens when people chase money and forget about people. Families and churches need to look after each other, because I don't trust government to.
S2.think: If robots can do everything, even the Brandts can't afford to keep me, because they have the bank to pay. I'd be 60 with nothing saved and no work in town.
S2.do: Goes back to sewing alterations and mending for parish neighbours for cash. Cuts heating and the car, and asks her son and the church hardship fund for help if needed.
S2.feel: Frightened, though she'd pray about it.
S2.quote: Two years, there's no getting to the pension, no getting to anything. I'd just be standing there with my sewing box.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI is the one picture where Bianca's loyalty network can't protect her, and she knows it. She'd fall back on her old trade, sewing, for parish customers. She reluctantly accepted she'd take state help she'd paid into, but prefers help from people who know her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd be 63. That's a bit better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing about families and churches. And I'd say young people should learn a trade with their hands, because that's what lasts. Though I suppose with robots, even that's not true anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means three years short of the pension. That's hard, but with sewing and Klaus's caretaking, we might manage. It's still frightening, but there's room to get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the sewing now, little by little, mending for the parish. I'd put that money away. I'd keep working at the Brandts' as long as they'd have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. But I'd feel I can get ready, a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd tell young people to learn a trade, then said that might not be true anymore. Which do you believe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose. I believe in trades, I was raised on it. But I'm not daft. If robots can do the hands-on work, then a trade isn't the safe place my father said it was. That's a hard thing to say out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at church would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Peters boy. He's 19, just started an apprenticeship as a joiner. His mother's so proud. I wouldn't have the heart to tell her.

S3.say: I'd say families and churches must look after each other, and young people should learn a trade with their hands. Though with robots, even that might not hold.
S3.think: Five years leaves me three years short of my pension. With sewing and my husband's caretaking we might manage, and there's room to get ready.
S3.do: Starts sewing and mending for the parish now and saves the money. Keeps working at the farm as long as she's wanted.
S3.feel: Worried, but able to get ready a little.
S3.quote: If robots can do the hands-on work, then a trade isn't the safe place my father said it was.
S3.fieldNote: When asked about the contradiction, Bianca admitted her lifelong belief in trades might not hold. It was clearly hard for her to say. Five years lets her start her sewing side work early and save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 68, at home with Klaus. That one's not for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's for the young ones to sort out, and that families should prepare their children. I'd say that at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad I'm old, God forgive me. I'd worry about my grandchildren, but for me, it would come when I'm already out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep going at the Brandts', keep my sewing up, see what happens. Maybe talk to my son about the little ones' schooling, later on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit sad for the young ones, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'God forgive me'. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's selfish to be glad you'll miss the storm. My mother used to say you should always think of the next ones. But I'm only human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your grandchildren?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That they keep their faith and their family close, whatever comes. Robots can't take that away. And that they learn to sew a button on, because some things you should do for yourself.

S4.say: I'd say at church that it's for the young ones to sort out, and that families should prepare their children.
S4.think: I'd be glad I'm old, God forgive me, because it would come when I'm out of it. I'd worry about my grandchildren, though.
S4.do: Keeps working at the neighbours' farm and keeps up her sewing. Waits to see what happens and may talk to her son about the grandchildren's schooling later.
S4.feel: Calm, a little sad for the young.
S4.quote: Because it's selfish to be glad you'll miss the storm.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lands after Bianca's pension, and she admitted a guilty gladness about it. Her hopes for her grandchildren centre on faith, family and self-reliance. She stays calm, rooted in her routine.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. There'd be no time to do anything but pray and sew. What would help is the Brandts being able to keep me on, maybe with some help from somewhere so small farms can keep their people, and the church being strong enough to help those who fall through.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. People think it's old-fashioned, but it's what holds a place together. When the factory closed, it was the church that fed people, not the government.

headlineQuote: Help from people who know you is different from a form.
portrait: Bianca Wagner is 58 and was a seamstress for thirty-two years until her uniform factory moved abroad; now she keeps hens and helps with sheep for the Brandts, the farming family from her church. She's slow with the sheep and learning from the farmer's 30-year-old son. She values work, family and faith, distrusts government help and never uses AI or computers. Her fear in slow change is being a burden to the family who took her in, and in fast AGI it's having nothing at 60 but her sewing box. With ten years she felt a guilty gladness that the change would pass her by.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she'd be out of work at 60 with nothing saved and no time to prepare.
whatWouldHelp: Support that lets small farms like the Brandts keep their workers, and churches strong enough to help people who fall through.
